after: ## Evidence is what stands behind a claim
alt: A claim, “the defendant took the money”, is supported from below by evidence (CCTV footage, a bank record, a witness) and by reasoning, the lawyer’s explanation of why the evidence together makes the claim true.
caption: Evidence supplies the raw material; reasoning explains why it supports the claim.

alt: Ten cards, one per type of evidence: fact, statistic, example, anecdote, personal experience, testimony, expert opinion, experiment or study, analogy and illustration. Each lists a strength, a weakness and the ferry example from the lesson.
caption: Recognise the kind of evidence, then explain what it does for the claim.

alt: A narrowing funnel of four questions: is the evidence relevant, accurate and credible, representative, and appropriate for the audience? Evidence that passes all four is useful.
caption: Relevant, credible, representative evidence that suits the audience beats a pile of weak items.

after: ## A public-domain example of evidence: Stanton's Declaration (1848)
alt: A stack of grievances beginning “He has...”, two quoted from the Declaration of Sentiments, bracketed together to support the claim that women have been denied rights. Notes explain that the evidence is a catalogue of concrete restrictions whose power comes from accumulation and from imitating a famous precedent.
caption: A catalogue of concrete examples persuades by accumulation.

after: ## Worked example 1: naming the evidence in an invented paragraph
alt: The invented ferry paragraph split into sentences. The first is the claim. The others are labelled as a statistic (late sailings rose from 12 to 68 percent), an example (the nurse who missed her shift), expert opinion (the chief engineer) and an analogy (a bicycle with a flat tyre).
caption: Only the first sentence argues a position; the rest can be checked or pictured.

after: ## Worked example 2: matching evidence to a claim
alt: Four pieces of evidence are aimed at a target labelled learning. Only (ii), a study of eight schools whose test scores were unchanged after two years, hits it. Popularity (i), one cousin’s testimony (iii) and a fact about where four-day weeks are used (iv) miss.
caption: The best evidence matches the exact thing the claim says.
